Learning Objectives
Describe the clinical presentation, including patient history and physical examination, of an
adolescent athlete with hip pain.
Identify the appropriate imaging studies for the evaluation of an adolescent athlete with hip
pain.
Review common conditions and treatment options associated with hip pain in adolescent
athletes.
Discuss outcomes and complications associated with the management of hip conditions in
adolescent athletes.


Overview
Developmental changes that occur during the peak height velocity in adolescents
present unique challenges to youth athletes who participate in regular competitive
sports or repetitive vigorous activity. Unique conditions of the hip present in adolescent
athletes and should be considered in evaluating hip pain in this patient population.
Epidemiology
6% to 12% of adolescents have hip pain.1,2
As many as 100% of ballet dancers may have some form of hip discomfort.3
15% of adolescent basketball players have hip pain and a positive impingement sign.4
19.2% of adolescent ice hockey players have hip pain.5
17% of skiers have some form of hip pain during training.6
5% to 9% of athletic injuries in youth athletes result from a groin strain.2,7

Epidemiology
In a cross-sectional analysis of German pupils, 6.5% had hip pain; however, only 2.9%
had hip pain during physical activity.2 In this study, risk factors for hip pain included
female sex, attending high school rather than middle school, and consumption of
tobacco.2 A recent meta-analysis demonstrated that the overall prevalence of short-term
hip pain (0 to 3 months) was 12%; however, this prevalence was as high as 31% in
patients with obesity and 100% in adolescents involved in sports activity. Siebenrock and
colleagues4,5 investigated youth hockey and basketball players with decreased hip
internal rotation and concerns regarding impingement. This authors found that,
regardless of the presence of impingement sign, 19.2% and 15% of the youth hockey and
basketball players had hip pain, respectively.
Anatomy

The hip joint is a ball-and-socket joint made up of the femoral head and acetabulum.
The hip joint has three degrees of freedom: flexion/extension, adduction/abduction, and
rotation.
The proximal femoral physis closes at approximately age 18 years in males and females.
Triradiate cartilage typically closes at age of 14 years in boys and age 12 years in girls.
Secondary ossification centers of the pelvis are the anatomic locations of apophysitis (overuse)
and apophyseal avulsions (acute).

Anatomy
Developmental anatomy of the hip and the pelvis in youth athletes is primarily focused
on closure of the multiple apophyses (secondary ossification centers) in the proximal
femur and pelvis. Parvaresh et al8 investigated CT scans obtained at a single pediatric
hospital to review the age of closure of these secondary ossification centers in the hip
(Table 1).


Risk Factors for Hip and Groin Injuries in Athletes
Multiple meta-analyses have investigated the risk of athletic groin injury.7,9
Overwhelming support suggests that inadequate rehabilitation and early return from
injury is a strong risk factor associated with recurrent injuries. Among systematic
reviews, the general consensus is that prior groin injury, reduced hip abductor strength,
and reduced sport-specific training are the key risk factors.7,9 Newer data suggest that
higher body mass index and reduced adductor strength also may contribute to hip and
groin injuries.10


Patient History
Adolescent athletes with hip pain commonly present with hip pain that is acute in onset
and typically associated with a soft-tissue injury or an apophyseal avulsion fracture. Most
of the hip pain associated with an insidious onset is related to overuse; however,
surgeons must not discount etiologies not commonly associated with youth athletes,
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:22 PM
AAOS | Hip Conditions in the Young Athlete
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000576
6/27

such as slipped capital femoral epiphysis, osteonecrosis (ie, Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease),
or infection (eg, septic arthritis, osteomyelitis).
The location of hip pain may be extremely valuable in narrowing the differential
diagnosis.12 Groin pain or pain associated with a C-sign (cupping of the hand around the
greater trochanter, finger anteriorly, thumb on posterior greater trochanter) was
thought to be intra-articular in etiology (ie, labral tear); however, other considerations
include anterior inferior iliac spine/anterior superior iliac spine apophysitis,
iliopsoas/rectus tendinitis, or impingement. Lateral hip pain frequently is extra-articular
and related to abductor pathology, greater trochanter apophysitis, or iliotibial band
pathology. Posterior hip pain commonly is from the gluteal musculature, secondary to
the sacroiliac joint, or from the lumbosacral complex
The presence of popping is a common finding in patients with internal or external
snapping hip syndrome or may be secondary to intra-articular pathology. Often, the
patient can visually reproduce external snapping hip on physical examination, whereas
internal snapping hip often is audible.


Physical Examination
A collection of comprehensive physical examination maneuvers to evaluate hip pain in
athletes has been described.12-15 With the patient standing, a gait assessment is
invaluable. An asymmetric external foot progression angle may be an early sign of a
slipped capital femoral epiphysis. A painless limp may be an early sign of Legg-Calvé-
Perthes disease, scoliosis, or leg-length inequality. A visual examination from behind will
allow for assessment of the lumbar spine, palpation of the sacroiliac joint, and
evaluation for pelvic obliquity. In addition, patients often can reproduce the snapping
from coxa saltans externa (external snapping hip) while standing.
Supine evaluation allows for visualization of the hip to ensure no signs of superficial
ecchymosis are present. Palpation of bony prominences allows for evaluation of pain
caused by an apophyseal avulsion or apophysitis—these include the greater trochanter,
anterior superior iliac spine, iliac crest, pubic symphysis, and ischial tuberosity. A straight
leg raise against resistance may reproduce pain if a hip flexor strain is suspected. The
flexion, abduction, external rotation test was originally described to distinguish posterior
hip/back pain from anterior hip pain; however, recent data suggest that a positive sign—
which is if the distance from the knee to table has a side-to-side difference of more than
4 cm—is associated with intra-articular pathology and/or impingement.16 An anterior
impingement sign is performed if the hip is flexed, internally rotated, and adducted. The
anterior impingement sign is associated with a high specificity (81.8% to 100%), with a
relatively low sensitivity (53.1% to 56.0%).16-18

The lateral or prone position may be useful in evaluating for hip instability. The most
common etiology for hip instability in this age group is decreased or insufficient anterior
coverage of the femoral head, which will produce an apprehension sign if the hip is
externally rotated and abducted.19 A positive sign is noted if the patient has discomfort
or apprehension. Pain alone also may be a finding consistent with posterior
impingement.
Imaging Studies
Radiography (Resource 2)
AP pelvis
Standing or supine
Lateral hip
Cross-table lateral view
45° Dunn view
False-profile view if instability or dysplasia is suspected
Ultrasonography
CT
MRI with or without arthrography

Imaging Studies
Radiographic assessment of the athletic hip should be performed systematically.20 A
standard AP pelvis radiograph with the patient in a supine position should demonstrate
a symmetric appearance of the obturator foramina, and the distance from the pubic
symphysis to the coccyx should be 1 to 3 cm (or the distance from pubic symphysis to
the sacrococcygeal junction to be a mean of 32.3 mm in men and 47.3 mm in
women).20,21 Some surgeons recommend a standing AP pelvis radiograph rather than a
supine AP pelvis radiograph to better assess the pelvic position during stance. Several
studies have established that the lateral center-edge angle (LCEA) does not change from
standing to supine positions; however, challenges in identifying retroversion on a
standing AP pelvis radiograph have been noted.22,23 An AP pelvis radiograph also can
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:22 PM

9/27

provide detailed information regarding the presence of traction apophysitis or an
apophyseal avulsion. The presence of the triradiate cartilage, the proximal femoral
physis, or the Risser sign may assist with knowledge of the skeletal maturity of the hip.
Lateral radiographs of the pelvis depict the morphology of the femoral head, which
commonly is associated with cam-type femoroacetabular impingement and also aids in
evaluating the position of the epiphysis (ie, in slipped capital femoral epiphysis) or the
height of the epiphysis (ie, in osteonecrosis). A 45° Dunn radiograph is the best single
lateral image to most accurately portray a cam lesion or increase in femoral head-neck
offset.24,25
MRI arthrography, compared with conventional MRI, is associated with improved
sensitivity (71% to 92%) in detecting chondral injuries or labral tears.26,27

Contraindications

Tönnis grade 3 or higher arthrosis
Hip pain in the absence of intra-articular pathology
Preoperative radiography, MRI, and CT are routinely performed.
Patient Positioning
Supine for arthroscopic approaches or open anterior arthrotomy
Lateral for arthroscopic approaches or for open surgical hip dislocation
Surgical Approaches
Most modern surgical management is approached arthroscopically; however, the surgical
dislocation approach can be used for deformities that are not amenable to arthroscopic
management (Video 1 and Video 2).
Labral repair should be performed with the use of suture anchors and is preferred over labral
débridement. Labral reconstruction rarely is indicated in adolescent patients.
Chondral pathology is addressed intraoperatively and consists of chondroplasty,
microfracture, or other cartilage-restoring procedures.
Acetabular rim trimming and femoral head-neck osteochondroplasty are performed, if
indicated.
The capsule is routinely closed.

Postoperative Management
Patients remain flatfoot–weight bearing for 2 to 4 weeks postoperatively.
A hip abduction brace can be used.
Physical therapy consists of progressive range of motion and muscle strengthening.
Pitfalls and Preventive Measures
Over-resection or under-resection of bone from the femoral head-neck junction or the
acetabulum is prevented by using intraoperative fluoroscopy. Evaluation of preoperative
radiographs is important to determine amount of resection necessary intra-operatively.
Complications
Continued Plan
Continued pain is a possible complication.
Fracture
Although no cases of fractures have been reported in adolescents, this may be a concern if too
much bone is removed.
Instability
Over-resection of bone or poor capsular closure may lead to iatrogenic hip instability.
Re-Tear
The labrum can re-tear if the bony impingement is not adequately managed, if micro-instability
persists, or if a patient returns to impingement of the acetabulum and proximal femur in
supraphysiologic positions.
Soft-Tissue Reaction
Tendinitis, most commonly of the iliopsoas, may occur postoperatively.
Neural Injury/Nerve Palsy

Outcomes
A recent systematic review of adolescent patients who underwent arthroscopy for
femoroacetabular impingement and labral tears demonstrated considerable improvement in
all patient-reported outcomes above minimally clinically important difference and patient-
acceptable symptomatic states. The return to sports activity rate was 85%.28

Outcomes
As defined by the Warwick Agreement in 2016, femoroacetabular impingement
syndrome is a motion-related disorder of the hip resulting in a triad of symptoms, clinical
signs, and imaging findings.29 It represents symptomatic premature contact between the
proximal femur and the acetabulum. The symptom of pain often results from injury to
the labrum from cam impingement and/or pincer impingement. In adolescents, cam
impingement likely results from injury to the lateral proximal femoral physis with
repetitive activity. Deep flexion likely exacerbates this injury. Inherent morphologic
differences in the proximal femur, such as femoral retroversion or decreased head-neck
offset, may contribute to cam development. The exact etiology of the development of
pincer impingement is less clear.4,30,31

Other Complications

Outcomes
Provencher et al32 reported on open Z-lengthening, noting a 88% return to active military duty.
White et al33 and Ilizaliturri et al34 reported 88% to 91% success rates with open and
arthroscopic techniques.

Outcomes
External snapping hip is a palpable and/or auditory snapping with movement of the hip
joint. External snapping hip involves the posterior iliotibial band or the anterior aspect of
the gluteus maximus as they travel over the greater trochanter of the femur during hip
flexion and extension or internal and external rotation. Usually, thickened portions of
the posterior half of the iliotibial band or the anterior gluteus maximus tendons not only
snap over the greater trochanter causing a catching or giving way sensation but also may
cause inflammation of the trochanteric bursa eliciting pain. This snapping often is visible
and reproducible.35,36

The most common reported complication is hip flexor weakness. Iliopsoas atrophy has been

Outcomes
Jacobsen,37 Dobbs et al,38 Gruen et al,39 El Bitar et al,40 Ilizaliturri and colleagues,41,42 Byrd,43
and Clark44 demonstrated improvement in 75% to 100% of patients; however, subjective
weakness was a substantial complaint in almost one-half of the patients.
Fabricant et al45 reported poor results after iliopsoas release in patients with femoral



Internal snapping hip most often is attributed to snapping of the iliopsoas over the
iliopectineal eminence of the pelvis. Other mechanisms include accessory slips of the

It most commonly involves snapping of the iliopsoas tendon over the iliopectineal
eminence or the femoral head with flexion and extension of the hip during external and
internal rotation. It usually elicits an auditory component and may cause inflammation of
the iliopsoas bursa.
Management of Hip Instability (Atraumatic)
Atraumatic hip instability is a condition that generally presents with an insidious onset of pain
rather than a sudden event. Although often referred to as micro-instability of the hip,53,54 this
condition commonly is observed in athletes with hyperlaxity or borderline hip dysplasia. This
condition may lead to chronic hip pain that may last for several years.55 In this setting, hip
dysplasia commonly is defined as a LCEA of less than 20° or an elevated Tönnis angle greater
than 10°.14,20 Pain may be associated with instability, chondral thinning, or a labral tear (Figure
2; Resource 3).
